index.html.text:
Bid Price Engine

Price any job at the profit margin you need. Enter labor, materials, subs and equipment, add contingency and overhead, and get the price, your walk-away number, and how far labor can run over before the job stops paying. One calculator for 120+ trades; pick yours for starting inputs and a link to its specialist calculator.

The job

Work out my overhead % from last year's books

Which margin wins the most money? Learn it from your own bids

A margin that looks right on the cost side ignores the bids you lose by quoting high. After each quote, log whether you won it. From eight bids with at least two wins and two losses, the page fits a win-chance curve to your history and shows the margin with the best expected profit per bid. The log stays on this device; nothing is uploaded.

Close out the job: what it really left

When the job is done, enter what it actually took. The bid above is the comparison. Closed jobs are kept on this device only; after three, the page shows how far your jobs run over and the contingency that would have covered it.

Questions

What is the difference between markup and margin?

Markup is the percentage you add on top of your cost. Margin is the share of the final price that is profit. A 25% markup is a 20% margin, and a 25% margin needs a 33.3% markup. This tool takes the margin you want and works out the price as cost divided by one minus the margin, so you never have to convert in your head.

How do I price a job so that I actually make money?

Add up what the job costs you in labor (wages plus payroll burden), materials (plus the waste you buy), subcontractors, equipment and travel. Add a contingency for surprises and your overhead, then divide by one minus the profit margin you need. That figure is the price; anything lower trades profit for the chance of winning the job.

What overhead and burden percentages should I use?

The defaults on the page are planning starting points for the kind of work you pick, not industry benchmarks. For burden, use your payroll taxes, workers' compensation and benefits as a share of wages. For overhead, divide last year's non-job costs (insurance, vehicles, office, software, owner's admin time) by last year's direct job cost; the helper on the page does that sum.

Does it work for my trade?

It prices any job built from labor, materials, subcontractors and equipment. Pick your trade to load starting inputs for that kind of work and a link to the specialist calculator for it, which models the details that are particular to that trade, such as dump weight for junk removal or squares for roofing.

What does the walk-away price mean?

It is your full cost: direct cost, contingency and overhead, with zero profit. Below it you lose money on the job once the business's own costs are counted. The cash floor is lower, only what you spend out of pocket, and is the figure to compare against a bid you are tempted to match in a slow week.

Is my pricing sent anywhere?

No. Every figure is calculated in this browser tab. Nothing is uploaded, there are no accounts, and a share link stores the inputs in the web address after the # sign, which your browser never sends to a server.

Is this legal, tax or accounting advice?

No. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type. It does not know your licensing, bonding, sales tax, prevailing wage or lien rules, and it makes no promise that a job will cost what you entered.

Guide: markup vs margin, with a conversion table. Running a trade with its own quirks? Every specialist bid calculator, by trade. Then send the number as a document with Estimate Maker, or test what price wins with Bid Win-Rate Optimizer.

No warranty. This is arithmetic on the numbers you type; it is not legal, tax, or financial advice. Defaults are planning starting points, not benchmarks. It does not model licensing, bonding, sales tax, prevailing wage or lien rules. Everything runs in your browser. Nothing is uploaded and there are no accounts. Anonymous feature counts (bid_priced, link_copied) stay in local storage on your device and are off under Do Not Track.

Install it: in Chrome or Safari choose "Add to Home Screen" (Android: "Install app") and it opens full screen and works with no signal on a job site. Building a store app from the same files: mobile/ README.

Free and MIT licensed. If it saves you a bad bid, support the creator on GitHub Sponsors.

markup-vs-margin.html.text:
← Bid Price Engine

Markup vs margin for contractors

Markup is a percentage added on top of your cost. Margin is the share of the final price that is profit. They are not the same number, and mixing them up is the commonest reason a busy contractor is short at year end.

A job costs you $1,000 and you add 25%: the price is $1,250 and the profit is $250. But $250 is 20% of $1,250, so a 25% markup is a 20% margin. If your plan needs a 25% margin, the price is $1,000 ÷ (1 − 0.25) = $1,333.33, which is a 33.3% markup.

Formulas

  • Price from cost and margin: price = cost ÷ (1 − margin)
  • Price from cost and markup: price = cost × (1 + markup)
  • Margin from markup: margin = markup ÷ (1 + markup)
  • Markup from margin: markup = margin ÷ (1 − margin)

Markup you apply → margin you get

MarkupReal marginPrice on $100 cost
10%9.1%$110.00
15%13.0%$115.00
20%16.7%$120.00
25%20.0%$125.00
30%23.1%$130.00
40%28.6%$140.00
50%33.3%$150.00
100%50.0%$200.00

Which cost to apply it to

Apply the margin to your full cost: labor with payroll burden, materials with the waste you buy, subcontractors, equipment, a contingency, and your share of overhead. Applying it to materials alone, or to wages without burden, leaves overhead unpaid, so the margin you quote is not the margin you keep. The calculator does the whole chain and shows the walk-away price.

Common questions

Is a 25% markup the same as a 25% margin?

No. A 25% markup on a $1,000 cost prices the job at $1,250, and the $250 profit is only 20% of that price, so a 25% markup is a 20% margin.

How do I price a job for a target margin?

Divide your full cost by one minus the margin. For a $1,000 cost and a 25% margin the price is $1,000 ÷ (1 − 0.25) = $1,333.33, which is a 33.3% markup on cost.

Which cost should the margin apply to?

Your full cost: labor with payroll burden, materials with the waste you buy, subcontractors, equipment, a contingency and your share of overhead. Applying it to materials alone leaves overhead unpaid.

Arithmetic only; not legal, tax, or financial advice. No warranty. Support the creator.
